<margin>
# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first point is clear. There is no doubt that, just as men can kill by God’s permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member or another. But in such cases, the demons do not act through the witches of whom mention is now being made. By these points, the solution to the second argument is also clear. But the claim that because God allows the generative power to be bewitched for certain reasons, it must therefore be allowed that such a member be truly and really removed, is invalid. It does not follow that this always happens, for such an event would not occur by way of witchcraft, nor do witches intend this when they perform such works, because they do not have the power to restore the member when they wish and know how. From this it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by <term>prestigiosa arte</term> <gloss>illusory or deceptive art</gloss>.

Regarding the third point concerning the wife of Lot, we say: her conversion was true and not by illusory art; however, we are now speaking of illusory art.

To the fourth point, that demons can induce some substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said, with regard to the magicians of Pharaoh, that they produced true serpents. Demons can indeed produce certain effects around imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do regarding humans, for whom God has greater care. This is according to the text: "Is God concerned about oxen?" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:9</note>. Nevertheless, as has been said, they can always, by God’s permission, harm humans truly and realistically, or even by illusory art. By these points, the solution to the final argument is also clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches work upon men by transforming them into beastly forms through illusory art.
</margin>

Fourth, the truth itself is clarified, where it is also said that they transform men into beasts. Concerning how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. From the 26th Question, 5th Chapter, *Episcopi*, from the Council of Anquira: "Whoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or the worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is undoubtedly an infidel and worse than a pagan." And let us use the arguments of Saint Thomas in the second book of his *Sentences*, distinction 8, "Whether demons can impress themselves upon the bodily senses by deluding them with illusions." Where, first, he argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must be somewhere, yet it cannot be only in the sense, because the sense does not have any species except that which is received from things, and there is no true beast there according to the canon law cited. Nor, again, can it be in the thing that is seen, such as when a woman appears to be a beast, because two substantial forms cannot exist in the same subject at once and simultaneously. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen cannot be anywhere, no illusory deception can occur in the eye of the one seeing, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form.

Furthermore, if it is said that that form is in the surrounding air, this cannot be; both because air is not receptive to any form or figure, and also because one and the same air cannot always remain around that person due to its fluidity, especially when they are moving. Furthermore, if this were the case, such a transformation would be seen by everyone, which does not happen, because demons are not seen to deceive the visions of holy men, at least. Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportionate to it. However, the active thing proportionate to the sense is twofold: one as if originating the act, namely the object; the other as if conveying it, such as the medium. But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor the medium conveying it. Regarding the first, that it cannot be the object: it cannot be taken from any thing, as was touched upon in the previous argument, since it is not in the sense as received from a thing, nor in the thing itself, nor in the air as a conveying medium, as was touched upon in the third argument. Furthermore, if a demon moves the internal cognitive faculty, either he does this by presenting himself...

<summary>This page concludes the refutation of arguments regarding the reality of demonic "transformation" of human limbs and beastly forms, asserting that such phenomena are not physical realities but illusory deceptions, while citing canonical authorities and Saint Thomas Aquinas to define the limits of demonic power.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft, illusory art, demonic illusion, substantial forms, Saint Thomas Aquinas, Council of Anquira, visual perception, canon law</keywords>
